lessons.title: What can my Chromebook do?
lessons.objective: Design a fair test, try it on your own device, and use evidence to explain what your device can do.

sections.title: A device is a tool with limits
sections.text: A computing device takes information in, follows instructions, and produces a result. Your Chromebook is a computing device. A keyboard sends letters in; the screen shows letters back. A capability is something a device can do. A limit is something it cannot do well in a certain situation. A device can be good for one task and poor for another. Today we will test typing and editing short text. We will not guess how fast every Chromebook is from one result.

sections.title: Make a test before you start
sections.text: An evaluation is a judgment based on evidence. Evidence is something you observe or measure. First name a task: type and edit a short announcement. Next choose criteria. Criteria are rules for judging success. Our criteria are: all the words appear, a change appears, and a button responds. A trial is one attempt at a test. Repeat the same test three times to see whether it works consistently. Keep the words, button, and browser tab the same so the comparison is fair. If you change two things at once, you may not know which change affected the result.

sections.title: Do the test and report honestly
sections.text: The typing lab below runs on this page. It does not send what you type to anyone. For each trial, type: Our club meets today. Then change today to Friday. Choose Check trial. The page checks whether the final text is exactly Our club meets Friday. after ignoring spaces at the ends. Record whether you saw the text appear and whether the button responded. If the page gives feedback, the button responded. If you mistype, correct the text and try again. A typing mistake does not prove the device failed. Do not enter your name or private information.

sections.title: Use evidence, then name a limit
sections.text: A useful conclusion names the task and the evidence. For example: this device handled short text editing because the final sentence appeared in three trials. This does not show that it can edit a long video. We did not test video. If something is blocked by a school rule, record blocked rather than calling the device broken. Do not change school settings or try to bypass a block. Ask your teacher for help. An honest incomplete result is more useful than an invented success.

example.text: Mina plans to test typing a club announcement. Her criteria are readable text, a visible edit, and a responding Check trial button. She uses the same sentence three times. In trial 1 she types Frday, notices the missing i, and fixes it. All three corrected trials pass. She concludes that her device can handle this short text task. She adds: I have not tested pictures or video. Her evidence supports the small claim she made; it does not support every possible task.

steps: Read the four short sections. Say the task and three criteria in your own words.
In the typing lab, type the original sentence, make the edit, and check each trial.
Read the worked example. Complete your evaluation in the response box.
Answer the practice checks. Use the reading link in feedback if you need a retry.
lessons.task: Write a device evaluation using these sentence starters: My task was __. My three criteria were __. I kept __ the same. In trial 1 __; trial 2 __; trial 3 __. My conclusion is __ because __. I did not test __. If a trial was blocked or failed, explain what you actually saw.
lessons.model: My task was short text editing. My criteria were that words appeared, the edit appeared, and Check trial responded. I kept the sentence and page the same. All three trials showed Our club meets Friday. and feedback. This device can handle this short text task because I observed all three criteria. I did not test video editing. Accept different truthful results; a blocked test earns credit if the student identifies the limitation and avoids an unsupported conclusion.
rubric: Names the task and all three observable criteria.
Describes a consistent process and three actual trial observations, including failures or blocks.
Makes a conclusion justified by the observations.
States an untested capability or another clear limitation.

questions.stem: Which plan gives the fairest comparison across three typing trials?
choices: Use the same sentence, page, and criteria each time.
Use a different sentence and a different tool each time.
Guess how the device will work without trying it.
questions.why: Keeping conditions the same makes repeated results easier to compare.
questions.evidence: Keep the words, button, and browser tab the same

questions.stem: All three corrected short-text trials work. Which conclusion does that support?
choices: This device can edit every long video.
This device handled our short text editing task.
No other device can edit text.
questions.why: The test supports the task actually tested, not an untested video task.
questions.evidence: this device handled short text editing

questions.stem: You type Frday and then correct it to Friday. What should you report?
choices: I corrected a typing mistake and checked again.
questions.why: A typing mistake is not evidence that the device failed.
questions.evidence: A typing mistake does not prove the device failed

lessons.title: Choose the right hardware + software
lessons.objective: Compare two hardware and software combinations and justify one choice using task requirements.

sections.title: Two parts must work together
sections.text: Hardware is the physical part of a computing system, such as a keyboard, screen, microphone, or processor. A processor carries out instructions. Software is the set of instructions a device runs. A browser and a text editor are software. A microphone alone does not make an audio recording: it needs software that can record. Software alone cannot record your voice without a working microphone and permission to use it. A combination is a hardware choice and a software choice used together.

sections.title: Start with the job
sections.text: A requirement is something a task must have. For a short typed announcement, you need a way to enter letters, a readable screen, and an editor that changes text. For an audio message, you need a working microphone and software that records sound. Our cards below describe fictional school devices and tools. Treat the facts on the cards as the evidence. These cards do not describe all real Chromebooks. Do not buy or install anything. Select a combination that meets every requirement before considering extras.

sections.title: Read the comparison cards
sections.text: Device A, the Classroom Chromebook, has a keyboard and readable screen but no working microphone in this fictional case. Device B, the Media Chromebook, has a keyboard, readable screen, and working microphone. Text Pad is browser software that edits text but does not record audio. Voice Pad is fictional browser software that records audio with an allowed working microphone but does not edit typed announcements. Both devices can open either tool. For a typed announcement, Device A with Text Pad and Device B with Text Pad both work. For an audio message, only Device B with Voice Pad meets all the requirements. The other pairings miss a required part.

sections.title: Weigh choices using evidence
sections.text: A tradeoff is giving up one benefit to get another. If two combinations both meet your requirements, choose using another stated criterion. In this activity, Device A uses less battery for text work than Device B; this is a supplied fact about the fictional cards, not a measurement of your device. If saving battery matters for the typed announcement, choose Device A with Text Pad. A newer-looking device is not automatically better for every task. Explain the task, the hardware, the software, and why another combination would be less suitable.

example.text: Owen must record a 20-second announcement. He compares Device A + Voice Pad with Device B + Voice Pad. Voice Pad can record, but Device A has no working microphone. Device B has one. Owen chooses Device B + Voice Pad because it has both required parts. He rejects Device B + Text Pad because Text Pad cannot record audio. He has evaluated combinations, rather than judging hardware by itself.

steps: Read the definitions and the fictional device/tool facts.
In the combination lab, try both tasks and compare at least two pairings for each.
Use the feedback to locate a missing requirement. Change one selection and retry.
Write a recommendation with evidence, then complete the checks.
lessons.task: A school club needs a typed announcement and wants to save battery. Compare Device A + Text Pad with Device B + Text Pad. Recommend one. Name the required hardware and software, explain whether both work, and explain your deciding criterion. Then explain why Device A + Voice Pad is unsuitable.
lessons.model: Both A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad meet the text task because each device has a keyboard and readable screen and Text Pad edits text. A + Text Pad is the better choice for the stated battery goal because A uses less battery for text work. A + Voice Pad is unsuitable because Voice Pad does not edit typed announcements. Do not accept an unsupported claim about real device battery life.
rubric: Identifies keyboard, screen, and text-editing software as requirements.
Evaluates both named combinations accurately.
Justifies A + Text Pad using the supplied battery criterion.
Rejects A + Voice Pad using the missing text-editing capability.

questions.stem: Which item is hardware?
questions.why: A keyboard is a physical part; an editor and instructions are software.
questions.evidence: Hardware is the physical part

questions.stem: Which fictional pairing can record an audio message?
questions.why: Only B has a working microphone and Voice Pad records audio.
questions.evidence: only Device B with Voice Pad

questions.stem: Both devices can edit text with Text Pad. The club wants lower battery use. Which choice fits the supplied facts?
questions.why: A + Text Pad meets the text requirements and the fictional lower-battery criterion.
questions.evidence: Device A uses less battery for text work

lessons.title: Solve problems one step at a time
lessons.objective: Use observations and one-change tests to find a routine problem, choose a safe solution, and communicate it.

sections.title: Describe before changing
sections.text: Troubleshooting means finding and solving a problem in a planned way. A symptom is what you notice, such as a sentence not appearing. A possible cause is a reason it might happen, such as a paused practice editor. These are different: the symptom does not prove the cause. Use our five-step process: describe the symptom; list possible causes; test one cause at a time; choose and check a solution; communicate the result. A test is an action that helps you decide whether a possible cause matches the evidence.

sections.title: Test safely and fairly
sections.text: Start with simple, reversible checks. Reversible means easy to undo. In our practice lab, look at the status and check whether typing is paused. Changing the practice pause control is safe. Deleting files or resetting a device would risk losing work and would not be a reasonable first step. Change only one thing, then try the original task again. If you change many things at once, you cannot tell which one helped. In a real classroom, ask the teacher about unfamiliar messages, permissions, or school blocks. Never bypass school controls.

sections.title: Find the cause in our practice case
sections.text: The lab is a simulation, which means a simplified model of a situation. It is not controlling your real Chromebook settings. The symptom is that choosing Send sample does not add a sentence to the practice output. The lab starts with practice typing paused. Check pause status: the lab reports paused. That supports pause as a cause. Choose Resume practice typing, then Send sample again. If the sentence appears, the original task works. Checking pretend Wi-Fi reports connected; in this case the task is on the page and does not need a network. Pretend Wi-Fi is not the cause. Reload case resets only the simulation.

sections.title: Compare solutions and tell someone
sections.text: Evaluate a solution by asking whether the evidence supports it, whether it is safe, and whether it solves the original task. Resuming practice typing is a better solution here than deleting files: the pause status points to the cause, resuming is reversible, and sending again checks the fix. A useful help message includes the symptom, tests and results, the chosen solution and reason, and the final result. If your test does not solve a real problem, report that honestly and ask the teacher. Do not claim success just because you tried something.

example.text: Jules sees no sentence after Send sample. Jules checks pretend Wi-Fi: connected. Jules checks pause status: paused. Jules resumes practice typing and tries Send sample again. The sentence appears. Jules reports: The sample did not appear. Wi-Fi was connected, but practice typing was paused. I resumed it because that matched the evidence and was reversible. Sending again worked. This message tells another person what was wrong and how the solution was checked.

steps: Read the five-step process and the safe-test rules.
In the lab, reproduce the symptom, check two possible causes, and read the log.
Apply the supported solution. Repeat the original task to verify it.
Write a help message and complete the practice checks.
lessons.task: Write a message to a classmate about the simulation. Include: symptom; two possible causes and the test result for each; best solution and why it is better than deleting files; what happened when you repeated Send sample. Use only results you actually observed.
lessons.model: The sentence did not appear after Send sample. I tested pretend Wi-Fi and it was connected; I checked pause status and it was paused. I resumed practice typing because pause matched the evidence and the fix was reversible. Deleting files would risk work and was not supported by the checks. I sent the sample again and the sentence appeared. If the student has not verified, send them back to the lab rather than accepting a claimed success.
rubric: Separates the symptom from possible causes.
Reports two checks and their observed results.
Chooses the evidence-supported safe solution and compares it with deletion.
Reports a repeat of the original task and communicates a clear result.

questions.stem: In the simulation, which statement is the symptom rather than a possible cause?
choices: The sentence does not appear after Send sample.
questions.why: A symptom is what you notice; pause and disconnection are possible explanations.
questions.evidence: A symptom is what you notice

questions.stem: Pause is on and pretend Wi-Fi is connected. Which first solution best matches the evidence?
questions.why: Resuming addresses the supported cause and is reversible.
questions.evidence: Choose Resume practice typing

questions.stem: After resuming, how do you verify the solution?
choices: Repeat Send sample and check whether the sentence appears.
Assume it worked because you pressed a button.
questions.why: Verification repeats the original task and checks its result.
questions.evidence: then Send sample again

lessons.title: Build a recommendation with evidence
lessons.objective: Combine your own device test, a combination comparison, and a troubleshooting report in one recommendation.

sections.title: Your client and the job
sections.text: A client is the person or group you are helping. Your client is a fictional school club. It needs a short typed announcement for a meeting. It wants readable text, editing, and low battery use. You have all the facts you need on this page. You do not need to research prices or download tools. Your recommendation will have three parts: evidence from your own typing test, a comparison of fictional combinations, and a troubleshooting message. Keep real observations separate from supplied fictional facts.

sections.title: Develop and carry out your own test
sections.text: Use the typing lab on your own Chromebook. Today you develop the test process before carrying it out. Choose one taught editing task: change a day (Our club meets today. becomes Our club meets Friday.), or delete a word (Our club meets today. becomes Our club meets.). You may choose another day word, such as Monday. Write your starting and final sentences, then write your own numbered process. Name the capability, your success criteria, what you will keep the same, and why three trials help. Criteria can include readable words, the intended edit, and a responding button. The final-text checker compares against your planned sentence; it cannot judge whether your plan is good. Carry out your process three times without changing it between trials. Record each observation. If you improve your plan, say what changed and start three new trials. A blocked trial is honest evidence too. Limit your conclusion to the short editing task tested.

sections.title: Compare the two combinations
sections.text: The fictional Device A has a keyboard and readable screen, no working microphone, and lower battery use for text work. Device B has a keyboard, readable screen, and working microphone, with higher battery use for text work. Text Pad edits text but does not record sound. Voice Pad records sound with a working allowed microphone but does not edit typed text. A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad both meet the club text requirements. A + Text Pad better meets the battery goal. B + Voice Pad would fit an audio task, but the club asked for text. These comparisons use the fictional card facts, not measurements of your device.

sections.title: Include a complete help message
sections.text: The practice editor simulation begins paused. Send sample shows no sentence. Check pretend Wi-Fi and pause status one at a time. Wi-Fi is connected; pause is on. Resume practice typing and repeat Send sample. When the sentence appears, the original task is working. Report the symptom, each test result, the selected solution and why it is safe, and the final check. The project is finished when another student could follow your explanation. Before you submit, use the four-part checklist below. Missing evidence means you need to add an observation, not a stronger-sounding opinion.

example.text: A complete recommendation might say: I chose to test deleting a word. My start is Our club meets today. and my target is Our club meets. My criteria are readable words, the intended deletion, and button feedback. I developed these steps: 1. Type the starting sentence in a trial box. 2. Delete today and its extra space. 3. Check the final sentence and choose Check trial. 4. Record what I saw. 5. Repeat in the other two boxes with the same sentence, edit, and page. Repeating helps me see whether the result is consistent. In my three trials, the words, deletion, and feedback appeared. This device handled my short editing task; video remains untested. For the club, both A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad can edit text. I recommend A + Text Pad because the supplied facts say it uses less battery. When the practice editor failed, Wi-Fi was connected but typing was paused. Resuming and sending again worked. I chose that reversible fix because the checks supported it.

steps: Complete three typing trials on this page and note your actual results.
Use the combination lab to compare A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad for the text task.
Work through the troubleshooting simulation and verify the solution.
Write the project response. Compare it to the self-review checklist, revise, and export it.
lessons.task: Write the club recommendation in three paragraphs. Paragraph 1: the personal device process you developed, including chosen edit, task, criteria, numbered steps, what stayed the same, reason for three trials, three observations, supported conclusion, and untested limit. Paragraph 2: compare A + Text Pad with B + Text Pad and choose using text requirements and the battery goal. Paragraph 3: symptom, two cause checks and results, chosen safe solution, and verification. Then revise anything missing from your checklist.
lessons.model: Use the worked example as the model, but require the student's own developed test plan and truthful three-trial evidence. Paragraph 1 must not treat fictional battery facts as a real measurement. Paragraph 2 must explain that both text combinations work and A wins the stated battery goal. Paragraph 3 must report Wi-Fi connected, pause on, resume, and successful Send sample after the change. Return missing parts for revision.
rubric: Personal evaluation: student-developed process with chosen edit, criteria, numbered steps, constants and repeat rationale; three real observations, supported conclusion, and limitation.
Combination evaluation: both pairs checked against hardware and software needs; choice justified by battery fact.
Troubleshooting: two causes tested, evidence-supported safe solution, and repeated-task verification.
Communication: clear enough to follow; distinguishes real observations from fictional facts.

questions.stem: Which project statement separates real evidence from fictional card facts?
choices: My typing test measured Device A battery life.
My typing trials checked text; the card supplies the battery fact.
Every Chromebook has a broken microphone.
questions.why: The typing test measures the text task, while battery information is supplied by a fictional card.
questions.evidence: Keep real observations separate from supplied fictional facts

questions.stem: Why choose A + Text Pad over B + Text Pad for the club?
choices: A can record audio with Text Pad.
Both edit text, but A fits the supplied lower-battery goal.
questions.why: Both meet the text requirements; the stated battery goal decides between them.
questions.evidence: A + Text Pad better meets the battery goal

questions.stem: Which message includes verification?
choices: After resuming, I chose Send sample again and the sentence appeared.
I clicked Resume and stopped checking.
I think every device problem is now fixed.
questions.why: The message reports repeating the original task and observing the result.
questions.evidence: When the sentence appears, the original task is working

lessons.title: Review, show what you know, and retry
lessons.objective: Use evidence to answer systems questions and explain a device evaluation, a combination choice, and a troubleshooting solution.

sections.title: Review: evaluate a device
sections.text: An evaluation is a judgment supported by evidence. First choose a task and success criteria. Then plan a test, keep conditions consistent, repeat it, and record observations. A trial is one attempt. Our typing test uses three trials of editing Our club meets today. to Our club meets Friday. The criteria are visible words, a visible edit, and a responding Check trial button. A conclusion must fit the evidence. Success with a short sentence supports short text editing, not long video editing. A typo can be corrected; it does not prove a hardware failure.

sections.title: Review: evaluate a combination
sections.text: Hardware means physical parts. Software means instructions such as a browser or editor. A task can need both. The fictional Device A has a keyboard and readable screen but no working microphone. Device B has all three. Text Pad edits text, not audio. Voice Pad records audio with an allowed working microphone, not typed announcements. A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad both fit a typed announcement. A uses less battery for text in the supplied fictional facts. B + Voice Pad is the only pairing that fits recording an audio message. Check all requirements before deciding.

sections.title: Review: troubleshoot and communicate
sections.text: Troubleshooting follows five steps: describe the symptom, list possible causes, test one cause at a time, choose and check a solution, and communicate results. In our simulation, Send sample produces no sentence because practice typing is paused. Pretend Wi-Fi is connected. Resume practice typing is an evidence-supported, reversible solution. Repeat Send sample and look for the sentence to verify the fix. Deleting files risks work and is not justified by this evidence. A help message includes symptom, tests and results, solution and reason, and the final check.

sections.title: How this assessment works
sections.text: Read the review and worked example first. Questions 1-10 are the unit knowledge test. Select one answer and choose Check answer for feedback. You can reread and retry; these are practice-friendly checks, not a locked exam. Your first checked answer and latest answer both appear in your exported work. The three-part written response shows how you use the ideas. A teacher reviews that response and your project evidence. The website does not automatically judge your writing or certify that you mastered a standard. Export your work before closing this tab.

example.text: A sample reasoning chain: The job is a typed message, so I need a keyboard, screen, and text editor. Both A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad fit. The client wants lower battery use, so I choose A + Text Pad using the fictional facts. My own three-trial typing test supports short editing only. If the simulation stops showing text, I compare Wi-Fi and pause checks, resume typing when pause is on, and repeat Send sample. Each claim points to a fact or an observation.

steps: Spend 5 minutes recalling yesterday's project, then 5 minutes reading this review.
Complete the ten knowledge questions in 15 minutes; use feedback and reread links.
Spend 10 minutes on the written response using your project observations.
Spend 5 minutes reviewing feedback and exporting your work for your teacher.
lessons.task: Use your Day 4 work and the review. A: Describe the personal device evaluation process you developed, including your chosen edit, numbered steps, constants, repeat rationale, criteria, three observations, conclusion, and one untested limit. B: For a typed club announcement with a battery goal, compare A + Text Pad and B + Text Pad and justify a choice. C: Write a troubleshooting message for the paused simulation with symptom, two tests and results, solution and reason, and the final verification. If you missed Day 4, open Day 4 and complete the labs before writing A and C.
lessons.model: A: Accept an honest repeatable typing evaluation with all three actual observations and a bounded conclusion. B: Both combinations support text; A + Text Pad fits the supplied lower-battery criterion. C: No sentence is the symptom; Wi-Fi connected and pause on are the checks; resume is supported and reversible; Send sample after resuming verifies. Score the written work separately from the 10-point knowledge test.
rubric: A: Student-developed task/process, criteria, fair repeated steps, three observations, evidence-based conclusion, and limit.
B: Both combinations evaluated with hardware/software requirements and justified battery choice.
C: Symptom, two evidence checks, safe chosen solution, and repeated-task result.
Communication: readable reasoning; actual observations; no unsupported general claims.

questions.stem: What should you choose before testing a device?
choices: A different device for every trial
questions.why: An evaluation begins with what to do and how success will be judged.
questions.evidence: First choose a task and success criteria

questions.stem: Which record is useful evidence for a short text test?
choices: Someone said all devices are fast.
The edited sentence and button feedback appeared in each of three trials.
questions.why: Specific observations from repeated trials support a judgment.
questions.evidence: repeat it, and record observations

questions.stem: The short text test succeeds. Which limit belongs in the report?
choices: Long video editing was not tested.
This proves every possible task works.
No limits need to be reported.
questions.why: Conclusions stay within the task tested.
questions.evidence: not long video editing

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly identifies hardware and software?
questions.why: Physical parts are hardware; the editor supplies instructions.
questions.evidence: Hardware means physical parts

questions.stem: The task is recording an audio message. Which fictional combination meets all requirements?
questions.why: B supplies the working microphone and Voice Pad records audio.
questions.evidence: B + Voice Pad is the only pairing

questions.stem: For a typed announcement with a lower-battery goal, which recommendation uses the supplied facts?
choices: A + Text Pad: both text pairings work, and A uses less battery for text.
B + Voice Pad: text editing does not matter.
A + Voice Pad: a microphone is not needed for editing.
questions.why: The choice meets the text requirements and then applies the battery criterion.
questions.evidence: A uses less battery for text

questions.stem: In the paused-editor case, what is the observed symptom?
choices: No sentence appears after Send sample.
questions.why: The symptom is the missing output; pause is the cause in this simulation.
questions.evidence: Send sample produces no sentence

questions.stem: Why test one possible cause at a time?
choices: To change as many things as possible.
To connect a change with its result.
questions.why: One-change tests help show which change helped.
questions.evidence: you cannot tell which one helped

questions.stem: Pause is on and Wi-Fi is connected. Which solution is best supported and safest?
choices: Resume practice typing, then send the sample again.
questions.why: Resuming addresses the evidence; repeating the task verifies the fix.
questions.evidence: Resume practice typing is an evidence-supported, reversible solution

questions.stem: Which help message gives enough information to follow the solution?
choices: No text appeared; Wi-Fi was connected and pause was on; I resumed and resent; text appeared.
questions.why: It includes the symptom, checks and results, solution, and verification.
questions.evidence: symptom, tests and results, solution and reason, and the final check
